guide.title: Learn
guide.subtitle: Plain-language answers about local AI models — what they are, what the numbers mean, and why they behave differently on different computers.

size.title: Model size
size.summary: What 1B, 7B or 32B means and why it matters
paragraphs: A model's size — 1B, 7B, 32B and so on — is the number of parameters it uses. A parameter is a value the model learned while it was trained; together they hold what the model knows.

Bigger models are generally smarter and more articulate, but they need more memory and are slower on the same computer. A 7B model can run on many laptops; a 70B model needs a workstation or a very powerful machine.
For most everyday tasks, a small or medium model is the right balance: fast enough to feel natural, good enough for chat, writing and coding help.
bullets: 1B – tiny and very fast; fine for simple chat and tests
3B – small; good for quick answers on modest computers
7B – the sweet spot for many laptops and desktops
14B – noticeably smarter; needs more memory
32B+ – high quality, but requires a powerful machine

quant.title: Quantization
quant.summary: How models are compressed to use less memory and storage
paragraphs: Quantization is a way of compressing a model so it takes less memory and disk space. The model's numbers are stored with less precision — a bit like saving a photo as a smaller file.

Less compression (Q8, Q6) keeps more quality but uses more space. More compression (Q4, Q3, Q2) uses far less space but can make the model slightly less accurate. Q4 is the most common balance and is what most people use.

Two versions of the same model can behave differently because they are different compressions. A Q8 version may answer a bit better than a Q4 version of the same size; a Q4 version of a big model can still beat a Q8 version of a much smaller one. The right choice depends on your memory and what you need.
bullets: Q8 – highest quality, largest files
Q6 – very good quality, moderate size
Q5 – good balance for most users
Q4 – most common: small files, small quality loss
Q3 / Q2 – smallest files, noticeable quality loss

ramvram.title: RAM and VRAM
ramvram.summary: System memory, graphics memory and unified memory
paragraphs: RAM is your computer's working memory. When a model runs on the processor alone, it is loaded into RAM, so the model must fit in the memory that is free at that moment.
VRAM is the dedicated memory of a graphics card. A model that runs on the GPU is loaded into VRAM, which is usually much faster. If a model does not fit in VRAM, it cannot run on the GPU.
Some computers — most Apple Silicon Macs and many recent laptops — use unified memory: the same memory is shared between the processor and the graphics chip. There, VRAM and RAM are the same pool.
What matters in practice: free memory, not total memory. A 16 GB computer with 12 GB already in use has little room for a model.
bullets: A model needs a little more memory than its file size
Running several things at once leaves less room for a model
GPU inference is usually faster than CPU inference

tokens.title: Tokens per second
tokens.summary: What tok/s means and how to read it
paragraphs: Models don't read text as words — they read it as tokens, small pieces of text (roughly one token per short word). Tokens per second (tok/s) is simply how many of those pieces the model produces each second.
Around 10–20 tok/s feels natural for a conversation. 30 or more feels fast, like a quick typist. Below 5 tok/s feels slow: answers arrive word by word.

In this app, speeds are estimates calculated from your hardware, not measurements. The only way to know the real speed on your computer is to run the model and measure it — that is called a measured result, and it is stronger evidence than an estimate.
bullets: 20+ tok/s – smooth, natural conversation
10–20 tok/s – fine for chat and most tasks
5–10 tok/s – usable but noticeably slow
under 5 tok/s – better to choose a smaller model

context.title: Context
context.summary: How much the model can remember while answering
paragraphs: The context window is how much text the model can see at once — your message, previous messages, and any documents you paste. It is measured in tokens: 8K means roughly 8,000 tokens, about 6,000 short words.
A longer context lets you have longer conversations and paste bigger documents. The trade-off is memory: the longer the context, the more memory the model needs while running.
The maximum advertised context is not always the best setting. Running at the maximum uses more memory and can slow the model down. For most everyday use, 8K to 16K is plenty.
bullets: Short context (4K): quick chats, short documents
Medium (8–16K): normal conversations and pasted text
Long (32K+): long documents and big code files

caps.title: Capabilities
caps.summary: Chat, coding, reasoning, vision and tool use
paragraphs: Models specialize. A chat model is good at conversation, a coding model at code, a reasoning model at step-by-step problems, and a vision model can look at images.
When you pick a use case in the app, we filter for models that are good at it. A model that is not marked for vision cannot understand a screenshot, no matter how big it is.

Some models can also use tools — for example, search the web or run calculations — when the app around them supports it. That depends on the software you use the model from, not only on the model itself.
bullets: Chat – everyday conversation and questions
Coding – writing, explaining and fixing code
Reasoning – difficult problems, thought out step by step
Vision – understanding images and screenshots
Tools – calling other programs when the app allows it

moe.title: Mixture of Experts (MoE)
moe.summary: Why a large model can still be surprisingly efficient
paragraphs: Most models use all of their parameters for every word. Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models are different: they split into many small specialists and activate only a few for each word.

This is why an MoE model can have a huge total size — 100B parameters or more — while needing much less memory than a normal model of the same size. Only the active experts are loaded and used at each step.

The trade-off: MoE models can be slower per word because the model must decide which experts to use. Still, they often deliver big-model quality on hardware that could never run a normal model of the same size.
bullets: Total parameters – the full size of the model
Active parameters – the part actually used for each word
MoE models often fit where a normal model of the same size would not

tags.title: Ollama model tags
tags.summary: How to read names like llama3.2:3b and qwen2.5:7b-instruct-q4_K_M
paragraphs: Ollama identifies models with tags: a family name, then after the colon a version or size. For example, in llama3.2:3b, the family is llama3.2 and 3b is the 3-billion-parameter version.
Sometimes a tag also carries the quantization, like qwen2.5:7b-instruct-q4_K_M. The exact tag matters: it defines exactly which file will be downloaded and run.
That is why this app always shows you the exact tag before downloading — the name, size and compression are all part of it. If the tag is wrong, you get a different model than you expected.
bullets: family:version – e.g. llama3.2:3b
family:version-quantization – e.g. qwen2.5:7b-instruct-q4_K_M
Different tags of the same family can behave very differently

license.title: Model licences
license.summary: Why you should check what a model allows
paragraphs: Models are published under licences that say what you may and may not do with them. Some are open and permissive; others restrict commercial use, or apply only to certain sizes.
This app does not give legal advice, but it shows each model's licence before you download. If you plan to use a model at work or in a product, check the licence text of the exact model and size.
The licence of a model is separate from the licence of the software that runs it. Both matter, but for different reasons.
bullets: Open licences (Apache-2.0, MIT) – few restrictions
Llama-style licences – free for most uses, some conditions
Some licences exclude commercial use or large-scale services

measured.title: Estimated versus measured
measured.summary: The difference between a guess and real evidence
paragraphs: Every model in this app comes with an estimate of speed and memory use, calculated from your hardware and the model's size. Estimates are useful for comparing models, but they are not measurements.

A measured result comes from actually running the model on your computer — the real tokens per second, the real memory use. It is the strongest evidence, because your hardware and settings decide the outcome.
After you download a model, you can run a readiness test in this app. The result tells you the model truly works here, which is more reliable than any estimate.
bullets: Estimate – calculated from hardware, useful for comparing
Measured – recorded from a real run on this computer
Measured always beats estimated
